title: Green iguanas in Taiwan: how pets became an invasive species

sources.publisher: Forestry Bureau (Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency), Taiwan
sources.title: Green Iguanas Pose Potential Harm to Ecological Environment. Rearing Must Be Registered and Breeding Only Permitted with Authorization

Number of invasive green iguanas growing
Registration now required to raise invasive green iguanas

facts.text: Green iguanas are native to Central and South America.
Green iguanas were brought to Taiwan as pets, and many escaped or were dumped by owners once they grew large.
Adult green iguanas can reach about two meters in length.
Green iguanas have no natural predators in Taiwan.
A female can lay dozens of eggs at a time (20 to 70 per clutch).
They mostly eat plants; in Pingtung they come down from bamboo to eat red bean shoots, even where farmers put up fishing nets.
Their digging may damage river embankments and can lead to road collapse.
Owners must register pet green iguanas, and breeding without permission is not allowed.
Counties pay hunters a reward for each iguana caught, and tens of thousands are removed each year.
Officials and experts say culling is unlikely to wipe out the iguanas completely.
Animal welfare groups have urged Taiwan to use non-lethal ways to control the iguanas.
Green iguanas are found along rivers and in parks in Kaohsiung and Pingtung.
